annotationRationale: The problem requires translating equal percentage-based team counts into a relationship between class totals. A linear equation and ratio allocation provide separate solution routes, sharing percentage-to-fraction conversion.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Prealgebra appropriately covers the percentage and ratio reasoning; no repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: Equal participation counts give j/4=s/10, so j:s=2:5. With j+s=28, j=8 and s=20; each class contributes two team members. Choice C and the recorded key agree. No figure conflict exists.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: Equation solving and ratio allocation provide useful, independently complete routes. Another choice-elimination route is unnecessary for this short problem. The unsupported seniors-choice shortcut in AoPS Solution 2 is appropriately omitted.
review.annotationCheck: cnm_p146 fits modeling the equality of percentage-based counts, while cnm_p195 is genuine shared conversion support. Precise equation and ratio procedures appear in the method tags. The question-level US links to 4.OA.A.3 and 6.EE.B.7 provide only limited modeling and simplified-equation overlap here.
review.areaCheck: Prealgebra appropriately covers the percentage and ratio reasoning; no repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The class totals are j and 28−j. Equating their team counts gives j/4=(28−j)/10. Multiplication by 20 yields 5j=56−2j, hence j=8. This gives 20 seniors and equal integer team counts of two.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Correctly credits LIVE and AoPS Solution 1. Replacing the references' two-variable setup with one variable and explicitly clearing denominators is a valid original presentation of the referenced strategy.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: Clearly connects equal team membership to the equation, explains both percentages, and displays the distribution and collection steps. No material transition is missing.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: cnm_045 fits contextual equation modeling, cnm_043 fits solving after distributing 2(28−j), and cnm_p196 fits expressing each percentage-based team count.

For cnm_043, A-REI.B.3 and 8.EE.C.7 are narrower, while 8.EE.C.7b, 7.EE.B.4a and A-REI.A.1 are partial. cnm_p196 supports the percentage-part portion of 6.RP.A.3/3c, not their complete scope.
nativeLayerJudgments.ailleo: All immediate IDs correspond to written steps and identify the precise equation route. Shared percentage conversion is legitimately covered by the percentage calculation node and question support tag.

methodReviews.mathCheck: For a common team count t, the class totals are 4t and 10t. Their ratio is therefore 2:5. Seven equal parts total 28 students, so the junior share is 2·4=8.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Correctly identifies AoPS Solution 3's common-team-count idea and develops it into an independently worded ratio allocation. It correctly places the eight juniors in the program, avoiding the reference's erroneous final wording about team membership.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: Explains why equal team counts produce unequal full class sizes, then justifies both the seven-part total and the junior share. The argument stands independently of the equation method.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: cnm_p198 fits recovering whole-class multiples from percentage parts; cnm_p187 precisely fits allocating 28 in the resulting ratio.
